source_refs.note: Book p. 50: 4.2.3 Scalar Multiplication (kA = [ka_ij]) with the pink Note box A + A + ... to n terms = nA. Worked illustration, Teaching notes, Key points and Common mistake are ours.

blocks.text: If \(A = [a_{ij}]\) is an \(m \times n\) matrix and \(k\) is a real or complex number, then the product of \(k\) and \(A\), denoted by \(kA\), is the matrix formed by multiplying each entry of \(A\) by \(k\), that is

blocks.text_alt: k A equals the matrix of k times a i j

blocks.text: Obviously, the order of \(kA\) is \(m \times n\).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: If \(n\) is a positive integer, then \(A + A + A + \ldots\) to \(n\) terms \(= nA\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A single number is called a scalar, to tell it apart from a matrix. Multiplying by a scalar never needs an order check: every entry is multiplied by the same number and the shape stays the same.
Our example (not from the book):
\[3\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3(1) & 3(-2) \\ 3(0) & 3(4) \end{bmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 \\ 0 & 12\end{bmatrix}\]
The Note agrees: \(K + K + K\) adds each entry three times, which is the same as multiplying it by 3.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Two special scalars: \(1A = A\), and \((-1)A = -A\), the matrix of negatives used in subtraction (4.2.2). Also \(0A = O\), the null matrix of the same order.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(kA = [ka_{ij}]\): multiply every entry by \(k\).
2. \(kA\) has the same order as \(A\); no condition on the order is needed.
3. \(A + A + \ldots\) (\(n\) terms) \(= nA\); \((-1)A = -A\); \(0A = O\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Multiplying only the first row (or only one entry) by \(k\), as with determinants later. For a matrix, every entry is multiplied.
2. Sign errors: \(3 \times (-2) = -6\).
3. Confusing \(kA\) (a matrix) with \(k + A\), which is not defined.
